title: I Wrestle with Longing for You, and Longing Wins
intro: Al-Wahidi says Kafur had sent al-Mutanabbi six hundred dinars. Ibn al-Iflili dates the recitation to Thursday, 2 Shawwal 347 AH (958 CE), during the celebrations at the end of Ramadan. A dark horse carries the poet from memories of those he left behind into a request for something money has yet to give him, an estate or a governorship. In return he can offer Kafur a poem that will enter tents as readily as walled houses.

translation: I wrestle with longing for you, and longing wins.
This estrangement amazes me. Reunion would amaze me more.
1.sharh: The Arabic puts the same root for overcoming on either side of “longing”. The next half doubles “wonder” in the same way. Both struggles leave him where he began, still apart.

translation: Will the days never err in my favour and let me see
someone I hate kept far away, or someone I love brought near?
2.sharh: He knows fortune's habits so well that a welcome turn would seem an oversight. Two people move in opposite directions and either change would be enough.

translation: God knows how little I lingered on that journey,
the evening al-Hadala and Ghurrab lay east of me.
3.sharh: He locates himself by the landmarks away to his east. They give the journey out of Syria a direction before the poet has explained why he is travelling so fast.

translation: That evening the kindest man to me was the one I forsook,
and the surer of two roads the one I shunned.
4.sharh: Al-Wahidi identifies the man as Sayf al-Dawla, the patron he has left. The better road may be the road back to him. Ibn Jinni also heard the choice of an indirect route to escape pursuit.

translation: Think how many favours night has done you,
giving the lie to those who follow Mani.
5.sharh: The argument borrows a simplified account of Manichaean dualism. A traveller can name specific good things darkness has done for him, starting with saving his life.

translation: It spared you death as you rode towards your foes.
In it the coy, secluded beloved came to see you.
6.sharh: Darkness helps the rider go out and the beloved come in. The second visitor ordinarily lives behind a barrier to other people's gaze.

translation: Many a day, long as a lover's night, I lay hidden,
watching the sun to see when it would set.
7.sharh: The lover conventionally complains of nights that never end. For a fugitive waiting for cover it is a day that feels like that night.

translation: My eye was on the ears of a white-blazed horse,
as though one star from the night remained between his eyes.
8.sharh: A horse's blaze is the patch of white on its forehead. His mount keeps a visible piece of night with him through the long day in hiding.

translation: His hide has room to spare around his body.
Across a wide chest it comes and goes.
9.sharh: The rippling hide is something the rider can watch. In the account al-Wahidi gives of horsemen's judgement, supple skin over a broad chest promises a generous stride.

translation: On him I cut through darkness. I draw his rein close
and he surges. I slacken it repeatedly and he plays.
10.sharh: The horse answers each adjustment with an excess of life. “Plays” lets the reader see something beyond obedience in the movement of its head and body.

translation: I fell whatever game I follow on him.
I get down leaving him just as he was when I mounted.
11.sharh: The comparison crosses the whole hunt. The horse he dismounts is still as fresh as the one he mounted before the chase began.

translation: Horses are like friends. There are so few,
though an untried eye may count them many.
12.sharh: The missing qualification is “that you can rely on”. A bystander counting animals, like someone counting acquaintances, has yet to apply the test he has just described.

translation: If all you see is their handsome markings
and limbs, the real beauty is hidden from you.
13.sharh: A blaze made the horse memorable to the eye. That visible mark alone would never have told the rider how it would fare after a hard chase.

translation: God curse this world as a rider's halting place.
Everyone in it with far-reaching aims is tormented.
14.sharh: The world becomes a spot where a traveller should be able to dismount. The very reach of his ambition prevents him resting there.

translation: I wonder if I shall ever compose a poem
in which I neither complain nor voice reproach.
15.sharh: The question is also about his trade. Even the poem he is about to offer as praise has already given him something to complain of.

translation: The least of what ails me would drive poetry away.
But my heart, daughter of the clan, is quick to turn.
16.sharh: Arabic makes “heart” and “quick to turn” almost the same sound. He calls to the young woman of the conventional love poem just as that change of heart carries him into praise.

translation: Kafur’s virtues, whether I set out to praise him
or not, dictate the words, and I write them down.
17.sharh: What began as the poet's own struggle changes into the fluent business of taking dictation. Kafur's character supplies words even to a reluctant writer.

translation: When you leave your family behind
and make for Kafur, you are no stranger.
18.sharh: He defines exile by how a newcomer is treated. This is precisely the claim that the lonely feast day a few verses later will put under pressure.

translation: He fills his actions with judgement and wisdom
and rare achievements, pleased or angry alike.
19.sharh: Good judgement often deserts an angry ruler. Here even anger produces a rare deed. One transmitted reading shifts the emphasis to the speed with which he responds.

translation: When his hand strikes in battle with the sword,
you see it is the hand that makes the sword strike.
20.sharh: Hand and sword swap grammatical places. The result of the blow tells a witness which of them supplied its force.

translation: His gifts grow more plentiful through delay.
The longer cloudwater stands, the more it dwindles.
21.sharh: The comparison with rain, usually praise enough for generosity, breaks down over time. There is also a gentle reminder that the poet has already waited.

translation: Abu al-Misk, is there a little left for me in the cup?
I have been singing all this time while you drink.
22.sharh: The guest who has provided the entertainment has yet to be passed the cup. The direct address lets a question about a drink carry a request for reward.

translation: You have given by the measure of our age's hands.
My soul asks by the measure of your two hands.
23.sharh: He agrees the gift was large by the standards of the age. Calling Kafur greater than his age creates a second and far more expensive standard.

translation: Unless you entrust me with an estate or a province,
your bounty clothes me and your business strips me bare.
24.sharh: An estate yields income and an appointment brings standing. A gift of clothes might be generous and still leave him dependent on work that takes all his time.

translation: At this feast everyone laughs with someone dear
in plain sight of me. I weep for those I love and mourn.
25.sharh: The festival marking the end of Ramadan brings loved ones together. He is close enough to hear the laughter and far from the people who might share his.

translation: I yearn for my people and long to meet them.
How can one who longs reach the far-off Anqa bird?
26.sharh: The fabled Anqa was known by name and beyond anyone's reach. The problem lies in the distance separating desire from its object.

translation: If it must be Abu al-Misk or them,
you are sweeter and dearer to my heart.
27.sharh: The choice is spoken in the patron's hearing. He names Abu al-Misk as if discussing a third party, then directs “you” straight to him.

translation: Everyone who does a kindness is loved.
Any place where honour grows is sweet.
28.sharh: Honour grows like a crop, a pointed image after the request for an estate. His affection is expressed through what generosity and a place to flourish can do.

translation: Your enviers wish you harm that God will ward off,
and brown spear shafts and finely sharpened steel.
29.sharh: The physical defences are named only after the divine protection. The poet does not even grant the hostile wish a concrete description.

translation: A horror bars them from their wish. If they could escape
from it into death, you would live, and a child would turn grey.
30.sharh: In this reading even death would offer his enemies an exit. The grey-haired child can express either the ruler's extraordinary survival or the terror confronting his opponents.

translation: If they ask your bounty, they receive it and name their terms.
If they seek the excellence within you, they fail.
31.sharh: The verb after “receive” lets the petitioners decide what they want. Naming an amount is possible. Acquiring the character of the giver is another matter.

translation: If they could possess your high distinction, you would give it.
But some things lie beyond giving.
32.sharh: The previous distinction is pushed to a paradox. Even a giver who would part with everything has something that simply cannot change hands.

translation: The most unjust of men spends the night envying
the very man in whose favours he passes that night.
33.sharh: The two repeated night-time verbs fit an entire moral contradiction into one night. The comforts in which the man lies awake have come from the person he resents.

translation: You raised the young ruler from his days at the breast.
He has no mother but you and no father.
34.sharh: Kafur cared for the Ikhshid’s son after his father died. The genitive on the studio card makes the child the holder of the kingdom. In al-Jurjani’s accusative reading, the kingdom itself grows up in Kafur’s lap.

translation: You were to him what the lion in its den is to its cub.
Your Indian sword was the only claw you had.
35.sharh: The guardian who took in the infant heir has the strength of a lion defending its cub. The detail that completes the likeness is a claw made of Indian steel.

translation: You faced the spears for him with a noble soul
that flees from disgrace into death in battle.
36.sharh: “Flees” initially sounds out of place in praise of bravery. The prepositions explain it. Disgrace is what he runs from, death what he runs towards.

translation: Death may leave alone the soul that does not fear it
and cut short the life that dreads it.
37.sharh: Death's choices refuse to follow the distribution of fear. The thought explains how the man in the preceding verse can seek the risk and still be here to hear the poem.

translation: Those who met you did not lack courage or strength.
The men they met were stronger and of better mettle.
38.sharh: The same encounter is described from either side. Granting the defeated men their courage sets a higher measure for the men who turned them back.

translation: He turned them back. The flash of swords on helmets came true
upon them. The flash of helmets on swords was empty lightning.
39.sharh: A small change of vowel turns bright blades into helmets. The swords make good their lightning with a shower of blood. The answering flash off the helmets promises rain that never falls.

translation: You drew swords that taught every preacher,
on every pulpit, how to pray and preach.
40.sharh: Naming the ruler in the Friday sermon was a public acknowledgement of power. Each wooden pulpit bears the consequence of a victory won elsewhere.

translation: What need have you of the pedigrees people recount,
when noble deeds trace their descent to you?
41.sharh: Kafur had risen from slavery and could claim no celebrated Arab tribal pedigree. The poet reverses the question of descent by making noble deeds his descendants.

translation: What tribe has the standing to claim all of you?
Ma'add son of Adnan and Ya'rub are your ransom.
42.sharh: The verb al-Nahari reads means to take something in its entirety. Even Maʿadd and Yaʿrub, ancestors of great Arab lineages, could scarcely claim Kafur as theirs. The early commentaries ask which tribe would be worthy to claim him.

translation: My delight on seeing you was nothing new.
I used to hope to see you, and delight would take me.
43.sharh: He says anticipation was already enough to move him. Al-Wahidi records an older reader's suspicion that the performance of delight could also sound like amusement at Kafur's expense.

translation: My rhymes reproach me over you, and so does my ambition,
as though I sinned by praising anyone before I praised you.
44.sharh: The listener has to wait to learn what the poet's own rhymes have against him. Their grievance makes his whole previous career sound like a breach of loyalty to his present patron.

translation: But the road was long. Time and again I have been
searched for these words and had them taken as plunder.
45.sharh: The verb is passive. He is searched like a traveller carrying valuables. Other patrons' eagerness for the goods accounts for earlier praise and advertises what Kafur now receives.

translation: It went east till the east had no further east,
and west till the west had no further west.
46.sharh: The verbs for travelling and the names of the destinations all come from “east” and “west”. The repeated words run to the edges of the map with the poetry.

translation: Once I say it, nothing bars its way,
no towering wall nor tent stretched taut on ropes.
47.sharh: The high wall stands for townspeople, the guyed tent for nomads. The rider earlier needed cover to get through the landscape. His verse can now pass any boundary on its own.

1.1.1.head: غالَبَ
1.1.1.meaning: Contend with an opponent for mastery. Longing can wrestle back.

1.2.4.head: الهَجر
1.2.4.meaning: Estrangement, the breaking off of contact between lovers.

2.2.2.head: ناءى
2.2.2.meaning: Keeps at a distance. The days are the subject, the unwelcome person their object.

3.1.5.head: تَئِيَّة
3.1.5.meaning: A pause or delay. The exclamation is about how little time he lost.

3.2.2.meaning: To the east of me. The places that follow are the things he locates.

3.2.3.meaning: Al-Hadala, a Syrian place named as a landmark on the ride.

3.2.4.head: غُرَّب
3.2.4.meaning: Ghurrab, a mountain in Syria paired with al-Hadala.

4.1.2.meaning: The most solicitous in his welcome. Al-Wahidi identifies Sayf al-Dawla.

4.1.6.head: جَفا
4.1.6.meaning: Treated him distantly or forsook him by leaving.

5.1.6.head: يَد
5.1.6.meaning: A favour, literally a hand extended in service.

5.2.3.head: المانَوِيَّة
5.2.3.meaning: The Manichaeans, followers of Mani. The poem invokes their association of light with good and darkness with evil.

6.1.4.head: سَرى
6.1.4.meaning: Travel by night, here under cover.

6.2.4.head: الدَّلال
6.2.4.meaning: A loved one's coy assurance of being cherished.

6.2.5.head: المُحَجَّب
6.2.5.meaning: Kept out of public view, secluded.

7.1.4.head: كَمَنَ
7.1.4.meaning: Spent it in hiding. The object is the day during which he lay concealed.

7.2.4.head: أَيّان
7.2.4.meaning: When, with the emphasis on the time for which he is watching.

8.1.4.head: أَغَرّ
8.1.4.meaning: A horse with a distinctive white patch on the forehead.

8.2.6.head: كَوكَب
8.2.6.meaning: A star, here the blaze appearing against the horse's dark head.

9.1.2.head: فَضلَة
9.1.2.meaning: Room to spare in the skin as it moves over the body.

9.1.6.head: إِهاب
9.1.6.meaning: Hide, the pliable skin over the mount's chest.

9.2.4.head: رَحيب
9.2.4.meaning: Broad or spacious, of the horse's chest.

10.1.5.head: عِنان
10.1.5.meaning: Rein, through which the rider makes contact with the bridle.

10.2.1.head: طَغى
10.2.1.meaning: Surges beyond restraint in high spirits.

11.1.4.head: قَفّى
11.1.4.meaning: Followed in pursuit, keeping on the quarry's track.

11.2.3-5.head: مِثلَهُ حينَ أَركَب
11.2.3-5.meaning: “Like him when I mount”, still in the condition he was in at the start.

12.2.7.head: جَرَّبَ
12.2.7.meaning: Puts to the test, whether a horse in use or a friend's constancy in adversity.

13.1.6.head: شِيَة
13.1.6.meaning: Coloured markings on a horse's coat, such as the blaze or white stockings.

14.1.1-2.head: لَحا اللَّه
14.1.1-2.meaning: “God curse”, an old imprecation related to stripping bark from wood.

14.1.5.head: مُناخ
14.1.5.meaning: A halting place where a camel is made to kneel for the traveller to dismount.

14.2.2-3.head: بَعيد الهَمّ
14.2.2-3.meaning: “Far-reaching in purpose”, someone whose ambitions allow little rest.

15.1.2-3.meaning: “Would that I knew”, an idiom introducing something the speaker wonders about.

15.2.5.head: تَعَتَّبَ
15.2.5.meaning: Voice a grievance or reproach someone for falling short.

16.1.3.head: ذادَ
16.1.3.meaning: Drives off or repels, as trouble might drive poetry from his mind.

16.2.3-5.head: يا اِبنَةَ القَوم
16.2.3-5.meaning: Daughter of the clan, a conventional address to one woman. The held vowel can sound plural. The caption and the metre support the singular.

16.2.6.head: قُلَّب
16.2.6.meaning: Quick to turn from one feeling to another. Qullab sounds like qalbi, “my heart”.

17.1.2.head: كافور
17.1.2.meaning: Kafur, the effective ruler of Ikhshidid Egypt and parts of Syria when the poem was delivered.

17.2.4.head: أَملى
17.2.4.meaning: Dictates the words for a scribe. Kafur's qualities do the dictating.

18.2.1.head: يَمَّمَ
18.2.1.meaning: Made for someone or somewhere, turning in that direction.

19.2.1.head: نادِرَة
19.2.1.meaning: A rare or exceptional deed. Another transmitted word suggests a spontaneous response.

19.2.2.head: أَحيان
19.2.2.meaning: At the times when, here in either of the ruler's contrasting moods.

20.1.6.head: كَفّ
20.1.6.meaning: The striking hand. The hand and sword exchange places in the wording.

21.1.4.head: اللَّبث
21.1.4.meaning: Delay or waiting before a gift arrives.

21.2.2.head: ماء
21.2.2.meaning: Waters, the accumulated rain from the clouds.

21.2.4.head: نَضَبَ
21.2.4.meaning: Recede or dry up after being plentiful.

22.1.1-2.head: أَبو المِسك
22.1.1-2.meaning: Abu al-Misk, Kafur's honorific name, used here in direct address.

22.1.6.head: فَضل
22.1.6.meaning: What is left in a cup after someone has drunk.

23.1.4-5.head: كَفّا زَمانِنا
23.1.4-5.meaning: “The hands of our age”, the scale of giving current in the world around them.

24.1.3-4.head: ناطَ بِهِ
24.1.3-4.meaning: Entrust me with something, literally attach it to me.

24.1.7.head: وِلايَة
24.1.7.meaning: A governorship, authority over a place on a ruler's behalf.

25.2.1.head: حِذاء
25.2.1.meaning: Right in front of me, within sight.

25.2.5.head: نَدَبَ
25.2.5.meaning: Lament aloud, as one might for someone lost.

26.2.4-5.head: عَنقاء مُغرِب
26.2.4-5.meaning: Anqa Mughrib, the fabled bird whose remoteness made it a proverb for the unattainable.

27.1.7-8.head: أَو هُم
27.1.7-8.meaning: “Or them”, his family. The syntax forces him to choose between two kinds of company.

28.1.3-4.head: أَولى الجَميل
28.1.3-4.meaning: Bestows a kindness or does someone a good turn.

29.2.1-2.head: سُمر العَوالي
29.2.1-2.meaning: “Brown spear shafts”, the upper portions standing for the spears themselves.

29.2.4.head: المُذَرَّب
29.2.4.meaning: Honed to a keen edge or point. The caption and diwan spell the word with dhāl. The recorded consonant has also been transcribed as dāl.

30.1.1.head: دونَ
30.1.1.meaning: Between them and it, introducing the obstacle to their wish.

30.2.2.head: المَوت
30.2.2.meaning: Death in this performance. Ibn al-Iflili's reading “to old age” imagines them surviving to go grey.

30.2.6.head: أَشيَب
30.2.6.meaning: Grey-haired. A child turning grey can suggest an immense lapse of time or a terrible shock.

31.1.3.head: جَدوى
31.1.3.meaning: Bounty or material benefit obtained from another.

31.1.5.head: حَكَّمَ
31.1.5.meaning: Were allowed to set the terms of their request.

32.1.4.head: حَوى
32.1.4.meaning: Take possession of something as their own.

33.2.4.head: نَعماء
33.2.4.meaning: The prosperity and benefits someone enjoys at a benefactor's hands.

34.1.4-5.meaning: The holder of the kingdom, here the Ikhshid’s son. The variant with a final a makes the kingdom itself the child Kafur raised.

34.1.6.head: مُرضَع
34.1.6.meaning: A child still at the breast. The passive participle describes the young prince Kafur took into his care.

35.1.3-4.head: لَيث العَرين
35.1.3-4.meaning: “Lion of the lair”, a protector defending its own cub.

35.2.4.head: الهِندُوانِيّ
35.2.4.meaning: An Indian sword, traditionally associated with high-quality steel.

35.2.5.head: مِخلَب
35.2.5.meaning: A beast's claw, here the sword that does the lion's work.

36.2.4.head: الهَيجاء
36.2.4.meaning: The heat of battle, with the usual final glottal stop dropped in the verse.

37.2.1.head: اِختَرَمَ
37.2.1.meaning: Cuts life short, carries someone off.

38.1.3.head: اللّاقون
38.1.3.meaning: Those who met you, here in battle. The Arabic condenses a relative clause into one word.

38.2.5.head: أَنجَب
38.2.5.meaning: Of finer mettle, with the implication of high worth and courage.

39.1.3-5.head: البيض في البَيض
39.1.3-5.meaning: “Blades on helmets”. Bid and bayd share the same written consonants.

39.2.6.head: خُلَّب
39.2.6.meaning: Lightning without rain, a proverbial promise that comes to nothing.

40.2.3.head: عود
40.2.3.meaning: Wood, meaning the wooden pulpit from which the Friday sermon is delivered.

40.2.5.head: دَعا
40.2.5.meaning: Pray for the ruler by name in the sermon, publicly acknowledging his authority.

41.1.3.head: نَسَبَ
41.1.3.meaning: Traces people back to their forebears and tribal lines.

41.2.2.meaning: Reach their ultimate point, as lines of descent converge on an ancestor.

42.1.2.head: قَبيل
42.1.2.meaning: A tribe or kin group to which a person might trace descent.

42.1.3.head: اِستَحَفَّ
42.1.3.meaning: Could claim all of you. Al-Nahari and the caption give a verb meaning to take something whole. The early commentaries have yastahiqquka, “deserves you”.

42.2.1-3.head: مَعَدّ بن عَدنان
42.2.1-3.meaning: Ma'add ibn Adnan, a traditional ancestor of the northern Arab tribes.

42.2.5.head: يَعرُب
42.2.5.meaning: Ya'rub ibn Qahtan, representing the southern Arab genealogies.

43.1.2.head: طَرَب
43.1.2.meaning: An access of emotion, here the delight of seeing someone long anticipated.

44.1.1.head: عَذَلَ
44.1.1.meaning: Reproach or find fault with me. The rhymes and his own ambition are made to speak.

44.1.3.head: قافِيَة
44.1.3.meaning: Rhymes, standing for the body of poetry he has written.

45.2.1.head: فَتَّشَ
45.2.1.meaning: I am searched, like a traveller carrying something highly desirable.

45.2.5.head: نَهَبَ
45.2.5.meaning: Is plundered, a figure for the eager appropriation of his verse.

46.1.1.head: شَرَّقَ
46.1.1.meaning: Went east. The travelling subject is now his poetry.

46.2.1.head: غَرَّبَ
46.2.1.meaning: Travelled west, as far as the direction itself can be pursued.

47.2.2.head: مُعَلّىً
47.2.2.meaning: Raised high, a wall substantial enough to keep an ordinary visitor out.

47.2.4-5.head: خِباء مُطَنَّب
47.2.4-5.meaning: A tent held taut by guy ropes running to its pegs.
